brief: Treasury's preference for funding via bills over longer-term debt makes it a de facto issuer of central-bank-like money, exposing the entire state balance sheet to the overnight rate and putting Fed independence, market stability and the real returns of stocks and bonds at risk. Bills are already above the Treasury's unofficial 20% ceiling of total debt outstanding, at 22.7% (24.1% excluding Fed-held bills), and are expected to rise further as the deficit widens. Because bills carry a zero haircut, they can be rehypothecated repeatedly without loss of value, unlike bonds. A cited 2015-2021 study found the collateral multiplier for Treasuries averaged three to five times. More money-like liabilities are structurally inflationary, and rising bill shares have historically preceded structural rises in inflation, a link the piece attributes to higher asset prices, a wealth effect and a repressed cost of capital. With more public debt tied to short-term rates, raising the policy rate now triggers automatic fiscal tightening, hamstringing the Fed, while cheaper bills push money market funds out of repo, raising the risk of funding flare-ups. The piece concludes no single rate can satisfy both the Fed's inflation mandate and non-destabilizing government borrowing.
